entry.title: OpenMeter: Giải pháp Open-Source cho Metering và Billing
entry.summary:
Building products that charge based on usage presents unique challenges, especially when it comes to metering and billing. Whether you're dealing with AI API calls, cloud compute minutes, or specific events within your SaaS platform, ensuring accuracy, reliability, and scalability is paramount. OpenMeter is an open-source project designed to tackle these very issues. It provides a robust and flexible framework for tracking usage metrics, enabling you to implement sophisticated pricing strategies without the heavy lifting of building such a system from scratch. Its design emphasizes seamless integration with your existing tech stack, making it an excellent choice for developers looking to create fair and transparent billing experiences for their users. Key benefits include: Reliable event ingestion and metering Scalable architecture to handle high volumes Clean integration points for billing systems Open-source transparency and community support If you're in the process of developing or refining a usage-based business model, OpenMeter is definitely worth exploring.

entry.title: Why POSIX Won Servers but Never Truly Won Desktops
entry.summary: At some point, every developer notices this pattern: And the obvious question follows: If POSIX is so good, why didn’t it win desktops the same way it won servers? The answer isn’t about quality. POSIX Was Born for Shared Machines, Not Personal Ones POSIX comes from Unix. This is basically the definition of a server. POSIX assumes: Servers look exactly like this even today. Desktops never did. Early Desktops Had Completely Different Priorities Early personal computers were: They needed: POSIX doesn’t optimize for forgiveness. Desktops needed forgiveness more than correctness. Servers Punish Mistakes; Desktops Must Survive Them On a server: On a desktop: POSIX is strict by design. Windows and Classic Mac OS allowed bad behavior because users demanded it. POSIX Is Text-First; Desktops Are Interaction-First POSIX assumes: This is perfect for: Desktops needed: You can build GUIs on POSIX but POSIX was never designed around them. macOS solved this by hiding POSIX, not exposing it. Backward Compatibility Matters More on Desktops Desktop users expect: This forced desktop OSs into ugly compromises. Windows chose: POSIX systems chose: Servers can break and be rebuilt. Servers Want Homogeneity; Desktops Are Chaotic Servers are: POSIX thrives here. Desktops are: POSIX assumes discipline. Why POSIX Eventually Entered Desktops (But Didn’t Take Over) POSIX did reach desktops quietly. But notice the pattern: POSIX is contained, not dominant. It’s there for: Not for: The desktop OS protects users from POSIX. Why POSIX Won Servers Completely Servers care about: POSIX delivers all of this. That’s why: Servers don’t need forgiveness. The Real Truth POSIX didn’t fail on desktops. It was never trying to win them. POSIX is a standard for environments where: Desktops are the opposite. They are personal, messy, forgiving, and human. That’s why: Different problems. Final Thought Operating systems don’t win by being elegant. They win by fitting the lives of the people using them. POSIX fits servers perfectly. And that’s okay.
